title: My personal interpretation of "The Boy and the Heron" (having seen it twice and read the book that inspired it)

commenti.body: [removed]

Absolutely gorgeous interpretation. It really helped me conceptualize this after watching it for the first time yesterday!! I really learned something, thanks.

Also! I wanted to add to the inclusion of all his old movies in this film. There’s a scene in The Boy in The Heron where there are insects flying around and all the bugs are from Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind! I had just finished watching Nausicaa before going to see The Boy and the Heron and was tickled when I noticed this.

I hadn’t thought about it that way. I was watching it wanting that Miyazaki magic of things like the past and didn’t watch it thinking about how this is the end of the magic. It makes sense thinking that way. I was on the fence of if I wanted to go see it again in theaters or just wait to watch it the second time at home on streaming, but your interpretation makes me want to go see again for sure.

You hit the nail on the head. 

Some additional thoughts: I felt like this film encapsulated Miyazaki’s grief over his mother, his grief over his dying kingdom, and finally the grief that the next generation will experience. The story concludes with our hero overcoming his grief through loving anew in the present. I think Miyazaki is telling us it’s okay to move on, and I love it.
[removed]

Your interpretation was fantastic and honestly makes the movie better. I personally wasn't too invested in the film (I feel like when they >!entered the below world!< the story got jumbled and off track) but I can see the artistic value even though it didn't really appeal to me 

But the art was still beautiful

I just got home from watching the film. I'm so glad someone else felt the way I did. I started crying when the Grand Uncle's world began collapsing. It felt like a final goodbye that I'm not ready for. Miyazaki's films have been a part of my life since I was a child. Now, as an adult, I appreciate them even more.

I kept seeing reminders of all his previous works throughout the film. Even the wall that the Grey Herron and Mahito are hiding behind to enter the blacksmiths home, it looks so much like the wall where Ashitaka encounters the demon boar Nago. 

Thank you so much for your very detailed analysis. It brought me so much additional insight (and joy). I can't wait to rewatch this film to find even more details I certainly missed.

I was thinking a similar thing. I noticed how much it mirrored Miyazaki life and thought it was probably similar since he likes to create worlds. very dark I loved it

Thank you so much for this! It really helped to conceptualize the film as a whole for me. I teared up when the film started just knowing that this was probably Miyazaki’s last film, feeling so lucky to bear witness to this handcrafted, meticulous, purely imaginative art. I felt a bit lost while watching, however this has solidified the film as a favorite, and I believe a second viewing is in order!

Amazing review, but I think not just the character of the great uncle represents Miyazaki Imo, Mahito also represents some of the aspects of Miyazaki for once hated the world and its ugliness for example war, but gain a different perspective while traveling the underworld and met with different companion now that he would call as friends, and finally answer to the great uncle that he himself cannot be the master of the tower, because he himself is also sinful, so he cannot make the any judgement for the world, cause no human should be the master of its kind.

Thank you for writing this up! Loved the video, too. 

According to Toshio Suzuki (longtime producer/colleague/friend of Miyazaki) in [this Indie Wire interview](https://www.indiewire.com/features/animation/boy-and-the-heron-miyazaki-anime-ghibli-1234927630/), the Granduncle character is based on the late [Isao Takahata](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isao_Takahata). 

Suzuki’s comments definitely shed some light on the Granduncle character and Miyazaki’s motivations and intentions for the role the character eventually plays in the story and how Mahito (Miyazaki) comes to the decision to take his own path. 

If anything, Suzuki’s words simply add another layer to this already deep and intricate story that I cannot wait to peel back and discuss for many years ahead. 

Thank you again for writing this up and sharing these amazing interpretations! 🦜
